content.text:
For most of human history, the written word was scarce. Books were copied by hand, and a single copy could take a trained scribe months. Monastic scriptoria, and later commercial workshops in university towns, copied scripture, liturgy, and classical texts. Still, the manuscript stayed expensive, full of copying errors, and limited in how far it could travel. The printing press changed this so completely that a world without it is now hard to picture. Its history, though, was neither as sudden nor as much the work of one person as the familiar story of a single German goldsmith suggests.

Printing began in East Asia. By the seventh or eighth century, Chinese craftsmen were carving whole pages of text in reverse onto wooden blocks. They inked the blocks and pressed paper against them.
